summary: Clarifies security issues in versions 2 and 3 of NFS and describes how they use the RPCSEC_GSS security layer and Kerberos V5 for authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: A shared file cabinet needs better locks. This explains how to use a stronger ID-checking system with it.

questions: what are krb5 krb5i and krb5p
is port monitoring secure for nfs
subtitle: What is weak about NFS version 2 and 3 security, and how NFS uses RPCSEC_GSS and Kerberos V5 to fix it.

tldr.problem: NFS versions 2 and 3 were commonly protected by weak habits such as trusting source ports below 1024 or UNIX user and group numbers, and there was no agreed way to use RPCSEC_GSS or Kerberos V5 with NFS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the weaknesses and gives SHOULD-level advice. It then defines pseudo flavors, 32-bit numbers that stand for a mechanism, protection level and service, so MOUNT version 3 can offer RPCSEC_GSS choices, and it registers three for Kerberos V5.
tldr.outcome: Implementers get compatible rules for NFS over RPCSEC_GSS and Kerberos V5, including the krb5, krb5i and krb5p flavors. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 2623 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers NFS versions 2 and 3 only.

sections.title: Scope and RPC Security Flavors
sections.content:
RFC 2623 covers NFS versions 2 and 3 only. NFS runs over ONC RPC, and every RPC call carries a slot for security parameters called an authentication flavor. A server may support several flavors at once. The RFC summarizes the known ones: AUTH_NONE (no authentication), AUTH_SYS (a UNIX-style user ID, group ID and supplemental group IDs), AUTH_DH (DES-encrypted parameters with Diffie-Hellman session keys), AUTH_KERB4 (the same with Kerberos Version 4) and the newer RPCSEC_GSS, specified in RFC 2203, which lets RPC applications use any GSS-API security mechanism.

The purpose of the document is to clarify NFS security issues, specify how NFS uses RPCSEC_GSS and describe how NFS works over Kerberos V5. NFS is not limited to the five flavors named.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request to the file server carries an ID badge. There are several kinds of badge, from none at all to ones with strong locks.

sections.title: Port Monitoring and Weak Flavors
sections.content:
Many NFS servers require requests to come from a TCP or UDP source port below 1024, on the theory that binding such ports is a privileged action on the client. The RFC says the theory breaks down: many operating systems do not restrict ports, and on a single-user desktop the user may know the root password or have physical access. Port monitoring is at best an inconvenience to an attacker and SHOULD NOT be depended on, though in rare cases of trusted, physically protected clients it MAY be reliable.

To keep things interoperable, clients SHOULD try to bind to ports below 1024, servers that monitor ports SHOULD provide a way to turn it off, and servers SHOULD NOT reject NULL procedure requests either way. The same advice applies to the MOUNT protocol.

With AUTH_SYS the server trusts user and group identifiers sent by the client, so client and server must share an identifier space or map identifiers. AUTH_DH and AUTH_KERB4 use network-wide names and encryption, so an attacker needs another user's network password or private key. RPCSEC_GSS uses a mechanism-specific principal name and cryptographic protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking which door someone came in through is not a real ID check, because anyone with the right tools can use that door. Real badges are harder to fake.

sections.title: Procedures, Exports and Access Checks
sections.content:
The NULL procedure is how clients ping an NFS server. Some servers demand a low source port or a flavor stronger than AUTH_SYS, but RPCSEC_GSS itself uses NULL for control messages. Servers SHOULD accept NULL over AUTH_NONE and AUTH_SYS as well as other flavors, and SHOULD NOT require a source port below 1024.

At mount time, a client acting as an administrative user often has no strong credentials, for example under an automounter. So some servers skip authentication for GETATTR and STATFS in version 2, and FSINFO in version 3. The RFC calls this an OPTIONAL trade-off: an attacker could only learn file or file system attributes.

Servers MAY bind flavors to exports and either reject a request using another flavor or map the user to a limited one such as nobody. Some servers check host-based access only at mount time, which means access cannot be revoked afterwards and a stolen or guessed file handle gets around the check. WebNFS public file handle lookups skip MOUNT entirely. Servers SHOULD therefore check authorization on each NFS request.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking the front desk whether the building is open needs no badge. But once you are in, the guard should keep checking your badge, not just look at it at the door.

sections.title: Flavor Negotiation and Pseudo Flavors
sections.content:
NFS version 2 had no security flavor negotiation, so clients guessed or used prior knowledge. The MOUNT version 3 reply to the MNT procedure includes a list of flavors. A client SHOULD use the first flavor it supports, and servers SHOULD list the best-access flavor first or let the administrator control the order.

Returning plain RPCSEC_GSS would not help, because it hides many styles of security: mechanisms times quality of protection (QOP) values times three services (authentication, integrity, privacy). The RFC introduces pseudo flavors, 32-bit integers from the same number space as ordinary flavors, each mapping to a triple of mechanism, QOP and service. Integrity includes authentication, and privacy includes integrity. A MOUNT version 3 server returns pseudo flavors instead of RPCSEC_GSS.

The server principal MUST be a GSS_C_NT_HOSTBASED_SERVICE name of the form service@hostname, with the service being nfs. Once a context is set up, the server MAY lock the triple for the session, since re-checking exports per message is costly and could enable a CPU denial of service attack, and clients SHOULD NOT assume they can change it.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of saying only that a badge is needed, the server hands out a short menu of exact badge types, each with a number, so the visitor can pick one.

sections.title: NFS over Kerberos V5
sections.content:
NFS uses Kerberos V5 through RPCSEC_GSS, with the mechanism described in RFC 1964. That RFC defines three integrity algorithms, DES MAC MD5, MD2.5 and DES-MAC. It says MD2.5 may be significantly weaker and DES-MAC may not be present everywhere, so NFS over Kerberos V5 is limited to DES MAC MD5. Clients and servers MUST support DES MAC MD5 and SHOULD support the single privacy algorithm, 56 bit DES.

The default QOP of zero means different things in different implementations, and at least one reference implementation always returns QOP zero when verifying tokens, hiding the algorithm in use. An implementation for NFS MUST NOT do that. Some mechanisms MAY simply map QOP 0 to DES MAC MD5.

The RFC registers three pseudo flavors, all with mechanism OID 1.2.840.113554.1.2.2: 390003 (krb5, authentication only), 390004 (krb5i, integrity) and 390005 (krb5p, privacy). Registrants SHOULD register the mapping with IANA, including a reference to an RFC and to the GSS-API mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three levels of protection: a sealed ID check, a sealed ID check plus a tamper-proof sticker on every message, and finally putting every message inside a locked box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MOUNT version 3 is used to negotiate the flavor for an NFS version 3 client. If the client asks the MOUNT server using a weak flavor such as AUTH_SYS, an attacker in the middle can coax the client into a weaker form of security than the real server requires. The server would still reject unacceptable requests, so at worst this is a denial of service.

If client and server share several flavors and the client prefers one, an attacker could push it onto the weaker one unless the client used a strong flavor for the MOUNT query. A client could contact the MOUNT server with a stronger flavor, but needs to know in advance which ones the server supports.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask the front desk for the list of allowed badges using a fake-able badge, a trickster in between can change the list so you pick a weaker one.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC requires that each triple of GSS-API mechanism OID, mechanism algorithm and RPCSEC_GSS service map to a unique RPC flavor number, a pseudo flavor that never appears in an RPC header, and encourages an ASCII string name too. Pseudo flavor numbers come from the same space as RPC security flavors, so existing IANA practice applies. Currently assigned string names include none, sys, dh and krb4.

String names have no length limit, so IANA may want the registrant to give the OID, QOP, service and flavor number to prevent name hoarding, and may want legal review because names can be trademarks. OIDs and algorithm values are assumed to be already allocated, and no guidance is needed for the three RPCSEC_GSS services.
sections.plainLanguage: New badge types and their short nicknames are written in one official list so no two badges ever share a number or a name.
